verses.zh: （亚萨的诗。）　神啊，外邦人进入你的产业，污秽你的圣殿，使耶路撒冷变成荒堆，
verses.en: A psalm of Asaph.O God, foreigners[NOTE:1] have invaded your chosen land;[NOTE:2] they have polluted your holy templeand turned Jerusalem[NOTE:3] into a heap of ruins.
notes: Psalm 79. The author laments how the invading nations have destroyed the temple and city of Jerusalem. He asks God to forgive his people and to pour out his vengeance on those who have mistreated them.
Or “nations.”
Heb “have come into your inheritance.”

verses.zh: 把你仆人的尸首交与天空的飞鸟为食，把你圣民的肉交与地上的野兽，
verses.en: They have given the corpses of your servantsto the birds of the sky,[NOTE:1] the flesh of your loyal followersto the beasts of the earth.
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

verses.zh: 在耶路撒冷周围流他们的血如水，无人葬埋。
verses.en: They have made their blood flow like waterall around Jerusalem, and there is no one to bury them.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “[as] food for the birds of the sky.”

verses.zh: 我们成为邻国的羞辱，成为我们四围人的嗤笑讥刺。
verses.en: We have become an object of disdain to our neighbors;those who live on our borders taunt and insult us.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “they have poured out their blood like water, all around Jerusalem, and there is no one burying.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，这到几时呢？你要动怒到永远吗？你的愤恨要如火焚烧吗？
verses.en: How long will this go on, O Lord?[NOTE:1] Will you stay angry forever?How long will your rage[NOTE:2] burn like fire?
notes: Heb “an [object of] taunting and [of] mockery to those around us.” See Ps 44:13.
Heb “How long, O Lord?”

verses.zh: 愿你将你的忿怒倒在那不认识你的外邦和那不求告你名的国度。
verses.en: Pour out your anger on the nations that do not acknowledge you,[NOTE:1] on the kingdoms that do not pray to you.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “jealous anger.”
Heb “which do not know you.” Here the Hebrew term “know” means “acknowledge the authority of.”

verses.zh: 因为他们吞了雅各，把他的住处变为荒场。
verses.en: For they have devoured Jacoband destroyed his home.

verses.zh: 求你不要记念我们先祖的罪孽，向我们追讨；愿你的慈悲快迎着我们，因为我们落到极卑微的地步。
verses.en: Do not hold us accountable for the sins of earlier generations.[NOTE:1] Quickly send your compassion our way,[NOTE:2] for we are in serious trouble.[NOTE:3]
notes: The kingdoms that do not pray to you. The people of these kingdoms pray to other gods, not the Lord because they do not recognize his authority over them.

Heb “do not remember against us sins, former.” Some understand “former” as an attributive adjective modifying sins, “former [i.e., chronologically prior] sins” (see BDB 911 s.v. רִאשׁוֹן). The present translation assumes that רִאשֹׁנִים (riʾshonim, “former”) here refers to those who lived formerly, that is, the people’s ancestors (see Lam 5:7). The word is used in this way in Lev 26:45; Deut 19:14 and Eccl 1:11.
Heb “may your compassion quickly confront us.” The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive, indicating a tone of prayer.

verses.zh: 拯救我们的　神啊，求你因你名的荣耀帮助我们！为你名的缘故搭救我们，赦免我们的罪。
verses.en: Help us, O God, our deliverer!For the sake of your glorious reputation,[NOTE:1] rescue us.Forgive our sins for the sake of your reputation.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “for we are very low.”
Heb “the glory of your name.” Here and in the following line “name” stands metonymically for God’s reputation.

verses.zh: 为何容外邦人说他们的　神在哪里呢？愿你使外邦人知道你在我们眼前伸你仆人流血的冤。
verses.en: Why should the nations say, “Where is their God?”Before our very eyes may the shed blood of your servantsbe avenged among the nations.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “your name.”

verses.zh: 愿被囚之人的叹息达到你面前；愿你按你的大能力存留那些将要死的人。
verses.en: Listen to the painful cries of the prisoners.[NOTE:1] Use your great strength to set free those condemned to die.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “may it be known among the nations, to our eyes, the vengeance of the shed blood of your servants.”
Heb “may the painful cry of the prisoner come before you.”

verses.zh: 主啊，愿你将我们邻邦所羞辱你的羞辱加七倍归到他们身上。
verses.en: Pay back our neighbors in full.[NOTE:1] May they be insulted the same way they insulted you, O Lord.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “according to the greatness of your arm leave the sons of death.” God’s “arm” here symbolizes his strength to deliver. The verbal form הוֹתֵר (hoter) is a Hiphil imperative from יָתַר (yatar, “to remain; to be left over”). Here it must mean “to leave over; to preserve.” However, it is preferable to emend the form to הַתֵּר (hatter), a Hiphil imperative from נָתַר (natar, “be free”). The Hiphil form is used in Ps 105:20 of Pharaoh freeing Joseph from prison. The phrase “sons of death” (see also Ps 102:21) is idiomatic for those condemned to die.

Heb “Return to our neighbors sevenfold into their lap.” The number seven is used rhetorically to express the thorough nature of the action. For other rhetorical/figurative uses of the Hebrew phrase שִׁבְעָתַיִם (shivʿatayim, “seven times”) see Gen 4:15, 24; Ps 12:6; Prov 6:31; Isa 30:26.

verses.zh: 这样，你的民，你草场的羊，要称谢你，直到永远；要述说赞美你的话，直到万代。
verses.en: Then we, your people, the sheep of your pasture,will continually thank you.[NOTE:1] We will tell coming generations of your praiseworthy acts.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “their reproach with which they reproached you, O Lord.”
Or (hyperbolically) “will thank you forever.”

READING CYCLE THREE (see

Bible Interpretation Seminar)

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in
the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in
interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the
key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has
one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 79:1-7

1O
God, the nations have invaded Your inheritance;

They have defiled Your holy
temple;

They have laid Jerusalem in
ruins.

2They have given the
dead bodies of Your servants for food to the birds of the heavens,

The flesh of Your godly ones
to the beasts of the earth.

3They have poured
out their blood like water round about Jerusalem;

And there was no one to bury
them.

4We have become a
reproach to our neighbors,

A scoffing and derision to
those around us.

5How long, O Lord? Will You be angry forever?

Will Your jealousy burn like
fire?

6Pour out Your wrath
upon the nations which do not know You,

And upon the kingdoms which do
not call upon Your name.

7For they have
devoured Jacob

And laid waste his habitation.

79:1-3 These verses delineate what the
Gentile invaders have done to the covenant people (PERFECTS).

- invaded Your inheritance (lit. "came in") ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal PERFECT

- defiled Your holy temple ‒ BDB 379, KB 375, Piel PERFECT

- laid Jerusalem in ruins (lit. "put," "place," "set") ‒ BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal PERFECT

- given the dead bodies. . .for food to the birds ‒ BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECTS, cf. Jer. 7:33; 16:4; 19:7; 34:20

- poured out their blood ‒ BDB 1049, KB 1629, Qal PERFECT, cf. Ps. 79:6, 10

- there was no one to bury them ‒ BDB 868, KB1064, Qal PARTICIPLE

The Jews could not understand how their God could allow the invasion of the land
and defilement of the temple (i.e., Habakkuk). It seemed to question His:

- power

- promises

- purpose for Israel

Psalm 79:8-13 gives the answer (cf. Dan. 9:1-14).

79:1 "O God" This is the first of several VOCATIVES.

- O God (Elohim), Ps. 79:1

- O Lord (YHWH), Ps. 79:5

- O God (Elyon), Ps. 79:9

- O Lord (Adonai), Ps. 79:12

The AB adds two more (p. 249).

- O God, Ps. 79:6

- O Scribe, Ps. 79:8

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, B., C., D.

▣ "the nations" The historical settings seem to be

- the fall of Jerusalem

- the destruction of the temple

- the exile of the remnant of the city left alive after the siege

This occurred in 58 B.C. by the Neo-Babylonian army (and its
mercenaries, PLURAL) under King Nebuchadnezzar.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

▣ "Your inheritance" Notice the number of times the psalmist accentuates
that the objects of attack belong to YHWH. By attacking His people, they are attacking Him. In
the ANE military victory was attributed to the victorious nation's deity.

- Your inheritance, Ps. 79:1

- Your temple, Ps. 79:1

- Your servants, Ps. 79:2, 10

- for the glory of Your name, Ps. 79:9

- for Your name's sake, Ps. 79:9

- Your people, Ps. 79:13

- sheep of Your pasture, Ps. 79:13

▣ "in ruins" This is a rare term (BDB 730) which is used twice in Micah.

- for the destruction of Samaria, Mic. 1:6

- for the destruction of Jerusalem, Mic. 3:12 (quoted in Jer. 26:18)

This Psalm seems to reflect the fall of Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar in 586 B.C.
(see 2 Kings 25; 2 Chronicles 36 and Lamentations).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

79:2 To be improperly buried was a horror to ANE people. To be eaten by animals was a
fearful prospect (cf. Jer. 7:33; 8:2; 34:20; Ezek. 29:5; 32:4-6; 33:27; 39:4-5,17-20). Psalm 79:2 is a
fulfillment of the curse for covenant disobedience in Deut. 28:26!

Notice in v. 3 there is no one left alive to bury the dead. This is hyperbole but surely true.
There was a terrible slaughter. The surrounding villages all fled to Jerusalem for safety and most died there!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

▣

NASB
"your godly ones"

NKJV, Peshitta
"Your saints"

REB
"everyone loyal to you"

NRSV, NJB, JPSOA
"your faithful"

LXX
"your devout"

TEV
"your servants"

This ADJECTIVE (BDB 339, KB 337) is based on the powerful
covenant NOUN hesed (BDB 338, KB 336), which denoted God's covenant loyalty!
So, the ADJECTIVE His faithful covenant followers (e.g., 2 Chr. 6:41; Ps. 4:4; 12:2; 32:6;
79:2; 89:20; 132:9; 145:10; 149:1,5; Mic. 7:2). In this context it is parallel to "your servants" in Ps. 7:2a. The
problem is identifying the person(s) that this refers to is Ps. 16:10, which seems
to be Messianic! I have included my exegetical notes from Ps. 16:10.

Psalm 16:10

"my glory"

NKJV
"my soul"

NRSV
"Your Holy One"

NRSV, JPSOA
"your faithful one"

NJB, REB
"your faithful servant"

LXX
"your devout"

NET Bible
"your faithful follower"

The Hebrew has "your godly one" (כבודי, BDB 339,
KB 337). This word is used often to describe

- those covenant people who loved, served, and obeyed YHWH (cf. Ps. 4:3; 12:1; 32:6; 86:2; Micah 7:2)

- when used of YHWH it is translated "kind" (cf. Ps. 18:25; 145:17) or "gracious" (cf. Jer. 3:12) because this
verse is quoted by both Peter (cf. Acts 2:27,31) and Paul (cf. Acts 13:35) to refer to Jesus' resurrection. In this
Psalm the term is translated "Holy One" (NASB, NKJV). I am not sure how to view this verse in the context of
Psalm 16. In context it obviously refers to a godly, faithful Israelite (note the parallelism of Ps. 16:10). It could
then have been understood by Apostles as Messianic

- prophecy

- typology

- multiple fulfillment

The Apostles looked back into the OT and saw many signs and foreshadowing, as well as
specific predictions, of the life, work, death, resurrection, and coming again of Jesus Christ! I trust their inspiration.

79:3 The first line of this verse

- may be an allusion to the ritual procedure where the blood of sacrifices was poured out at the
base of the altar of sacrifice after a small amount was smeared on the horns of the altar (i.e., Lev. 4:7;
Deut. 12:27). Jerusalem was destroyed as a ritual sacrifice and the bodies of the dead as a banquet for the wild animals.

- simply imagery of a terrible slaughter ("pour out," same VERB used in v. 6 as a
prayer request for YHWH to judge the nations)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIN OFFERING

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALTAR OF SACRIFICE

79:4 The covenant people have become

- a reproach (lit. "a taunt," BDB 357) to their Gentile neighbors, cf. Ps. 44:13; 69:9,19; 80:6; 89:41

- a scoffing (lit. "mocked," BDB 541), cf. Ps. 44:13; Ezek. 23:32; 36:4

- a derision, cf. Ps. 44:13; Jer. 20:8 (NOUN BDB 887, used only three times and
the VERB form four more in the OT)

This was exactly opposite to YHWH's purpose for Israel, which was to help the
nations know Him and come to Him (cf. Ezek. 36:22-23).

79:5 These three questions,

- How long? (cf. Ps. 13:1; 74:10; 80:4; 89:46; 90:13; 94:3)

- Will You be angry forever? (cf. Ps. 44:23 74:1; 77:7; 85:5; 89:46; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: JEALOUSY, ZEAL)

- Will Your jealousy burn like fire? (cf. Ps. 89:46)

are the focus of Israel's confusion and prayer. Has YHWH's special
relationship with the descendants of Abraham changed (cf. Ps. 89:1-4)?

YHWH has an unchanging purpose for Israel (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-30, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN), but they must remember that the
promises of protection, provision, and presence are conditional (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT).
Each generation must embrace and live out the covenant. Remember the Psalms are part of the OT's "two ways"
(cf. Deut. 30:15-20; Psalm 1).

79:6-7 This is a prayer ("pour out," BDB 1049, KB 1629, Qal IMPERATIVE) for YHWH
to act in judgment and deliverance (cf. Ps. 79:9) for His covenant people (cf. Jer. 10:25). Notice how the nations (BDB 156) are characterized.

- which do not know You (see SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW)

- which do not call upon Your name (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH)

It must be remembered that the nations

- do not have true revelation

- are controlled by the demonically inspired pagan idols

Israel was to be "the" channel of YHWH's revelations about Himself. It is not
surprising that the nations act in inappropriate ways (cf. Ps. 79:7). What is
surprising is that Israel, with all the spiritual benefits (cf. Rom. 9:4-5),
acts the way she does (cf. Luke 12:48)!

79:7 "For they have" The MT has "for
he has," but the ancient versions have "they" (LXX, Syriac, Vulgate). The change
involves only a revocalization.

▣

This root (BDB 627, KB 678) has several meanings.

- abode of a shepherd (i.e., Jer. 33:12) or person (i.e., Job 18:15)

- habitation of a nation (i.e., Jer. 31:23 ‒ Judah; 49:20 ‒ Edom; 50:45 ‒ Babylon)

- a city (cf. Isa. 33:20)

- remote military outposts (NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 55, i.e., Ps. 79:7; Isa. 27:10; Jer. 10:25; 25:30)

- habitation (i.e., the earth, cf. Jer. 25:30)

- place of rest (BDB 628, cf. Isa. 32:18 parallels)

Psalm 79:7 follows the usage of #2.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 79:8-13

8Do not remember
the iniquities of our forefathers against us;

Let Your compassion come
quickly to meet us,

For we are brought very low.

9Help us, O God of
our salvation, for the glory of Your name;

And deliver us and forgive our
sins for Your name's sake.

10Why should the
nations say, "Where is their God?"

Let there be known among the
nations in our sight,

Vengeance for the blood of
Your servants which has been shed.

11Let the groaning
of the prisoner come before You;

According to the greatness of
Your power preserve those who are doomed to die.

12And return to our
neighbors sevenfold into their bosom

The reproach with which they
have reproached You, O Lord.

13So we Your people
and the sheep of Your pasture

Will give thanks to You
forever;

To all generations we will
tell of Your praise.

79:8-9 Two significant issues emerge in these verses.

- Israel's prayer for God to remember His covenant

- Israel's prayer for God to not remember their continual covenant rebellion and disobedience (these covenant people
seem to be blaming their forefather's sins for their current conditions)

They base their prayers on the fact that the nations will misunderstand YHWH
(cf. Ps. 79:10).

These two verses have four IMPERATIVES OF ENTREATY
and two IMPERFECTS used as JUSSIVES.

- do not remember ‒ BDB 269, KB 269, Qal IMPERFECT used in a IMPERFECT sense

- come quickly ‒ BDB 554, KB 553, Piel IMPERATIVE

- to meet us ‒ BDB 869, KB 1068, Piel IMPERFECT used in a IMPERFECT sense

- help us ‒ BDB 740, KB 810, Qal IMPERATIVE

- deliver us ‒ BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- forgive our sin ‒ BDB 497, KB 493, Piel IMPERATIVE

79:8 Line 1 is an allusion to the
theological issue of the transference of sin (and/or blessing/forgiveness) to
future generations. In the Ten Commandments

- the results of sin are visited to the third and fourth generations (cf. Exod. 20:5; Deut. 5:9)

- lovingkindness to many generations of those who love YHWH and keep His commandments (cf. Exod. 34:7; Deut. 5:10; 7:9)

Both the effects of sin and mercy move through time and families but each is based on human choices!

79:9 "O God of our salvation" This
phrase is a repeated title for Israel's God (cf. Ps. 18:46; 24:5; 25:5; 27:9;
65:5; 85:4).

The BDB lists several ways the term "salvation" (BDB 447) is
used in the OT.

- FEMININE

- welfare, prosperity

- deliverance

- salvation from external evils (i.e., Ps. 78:22; 80:2)

- victory (i.e., Ps. 20:5; 21:1,5; 44:4)

- MASCULINE

- safety, welfare, prosperity (i.e., Ps. 12:5)

- salvation (usage here)

- victory (i.e., Ps. 20:6)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

79:10-13 Notice the two kinds of
people (i.e., Israelite ‒ Gentile). The Gentiles are ignorant of YHWH and they
act in inappropriate ways. Israel pleads for judgment in order that His people
may

- "give thanks" ‒ BDB 392, KB 389, Hiphil IMPERFECT

- "tell of Your praise" ‒ BDB 707, KB 765, Piel IMPERFECT

It is shocking to see the pain of the psalmist over the fall of
Jerusalem, the desecration of the temple, and the exile of the Davidic seed.
However, by faith, he can still envision a future time of praise!

79:10 "Where is their God?" The
nations ask a powerful question (cf. Ps. 42:3,10; 115:2). In Psalm 42 it is
asked by other Israelites but in Psalm 115 and here, by Gentiles. Are they
seeking information or ridiculing Israel's God? The second option is obvious
from the context but the first option is the ultimate purpose of God,

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

79:11 "those who are doomed to die"
This is a rare phrase (cf. Ps. 102:20). It could refer to

- those exiled survivors of the invasion

- those awaiting execution

- those kept from the temple (JPSOA footnote, cf. Ps. 79:13)

▣

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, LXX
"preserve"

JPSOA
"reprieve"

NJB, REB
"save"

NEB
"unbind"

TEV, Peshitta, NET
"free"

This VERB (BDB 451, KB 451, Hiphil IMPERATIVE)
is used in the sense of "release" only here. It usually denotes that which is left over and is superflous and, therefore,
can be disregarded.

The question is, "Does this refer to

- restore from exile

- restore from shame

- restore from death?

Some textual entities advocate a different Semitic root.

- left over, ותר (MT in Hiphil stem)

- free נתר, BDB 684 II, Kb 736 II, cf. Ps. 105:20

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM

79:12 "sevenfold" The number seven usually denotes "perfection" (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4) but here it denotes an
adequate (cf. Deut. 28:25; Ps. 12:6; Prov. 6:31) judgment (cf. Gen. 4:15,24).

▣ "into their bosom" The term "bosom"
(BDB 300, KB 312) is used in many senses in the Bible. Here it denotes the inner part of
a person (cf. Ps. 35:13; Jer. 32:18). The psalmist is praying for a complete
judgment on the Gentile invaders (i.e., Isa. 65:6,7).

▣ "The reproach with which they have
reproached You" The
NOUN and VERB "reproach" or "taunt" (BDB 357, cf. Ps. 74:10,18 and a similar root in Ps.
74:22; Lam. 3:30,61; 5:1) is used often in Scripture. The psalmist sees an
attack on Jerusalem as an attack on YHWH.

79:13 "the sheep of Your pasture" It
is interesting that in the Psalms of Asaph this theme concludes Psalms 77, 78,
and 79 (also note how Psalm 80 begins). It reflects the powerful, personal
truth/imagery of Psalm 23!

▣ "will give thanks to You forever" This is a round about way to pray for lthe
restoration of the temple and the psalmist's presence there. Thanksgiving was an integral part of worship!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THANKSGIVING

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

▣ "all generations" One wonders how this relates to v. 8. These current covenant
people were experiencing the wrath of God because of their sins and the previous generations' sins! But
they are looking/praying for a new day when faith, obedience, and praise move through their future generations.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide
commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of
the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible and the
Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a
commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think
through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be
thought provoking, not definitive.

- Why is 586 B.C. the best guess at the historical setting of this Psalm?

- Why was God angry at His people? In this Psalm who are His people?

- Does sin move through generations?

- How is Ps. 79:10 related to God's eternal redemptive purpose? (see

Special Topic: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN).

- How is Ps. 79:12b related to the prayer for forgiveness and deliverance?
